'''''Iris'' × ''germanica''''' is the accepted name for a species of [[flowering plant]]s in the family ''[[Iridaceae]]'' commonly known as the '''bearded iris'''<ref name=BSBIchecklist>{{cite web |title=BSBI List of British & Irish Vascular Plants and Stoneworts |url=http://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/uk-species/species/iris_germanica.html }}</ref> or the '''German bearded iris'''.<ref>Rudy J. Favretti and Joy P. Favretti {{Googlebooks|I9LR1XuKjMIC|Landscapes and Gardens for Historic Buildings: A Handbook for Reproducing and creating authentic landscape settings|page=145}}</ref> It is of hybrid origin.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles |edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=9780521707725}}</ref>{{rp|87}} Varieties include [[Iris florentina|''I.'' × ''g.'' var. ''florentina'']].

== Description ==
''Iris'' × ''germanica'' grows up to {{cvt|120|cm|in}} high and {{cvt|30|cm|in}} wide.<ref name="pacbulb"/> The roots can go up to {{cvt|10|cm|in}} deep and it is a rhizomatous perennial that blooms mid to late spring. Hundreds of cultivars exist representing nearly every colour from jet black to sparkling whites and red.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ashtakala |first1=S. S. |last2=Forward |first2=D. F. |title=Pigmentation in iris hybrids: Occurrence of flavonoid pigments in six cultivars of Iris germanica |journal=Canadian Journal of Botany |date=January 2011 |volume=49 |issue=11 |pages=1975–1979 |doi=10.1139/b71-276}}</ref> Some cultivars are known to re-bloom in the autumn (fall).<ref name=gardenia>{{cite web |title=''Iris Germanica'' (Bearded Iris) |url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant-variety/iris-germanica-bearded-iris |website=Gardenia.net |access-date=29 July 2021}}</ref>

===Phytochemistry===
It is known to produce the isoflavone [[irilone]],<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://cat.inist.fr/?aModele=afficheN&cpsidt=21235726|title=Lipase-catalyzed regioselective protection/deprotection of hydroxyl groups of the isoflavone irilone isolated from Iris germanica|volume=27|issue=2}}</ref> and several analytical studies have been made from the rhizomes.<ref>Shahid Akbar {{google books|oJneDwAAQBAJ|Handbook of 200 Medicinal Plants:  A Comprehensive Review of Their Traditional Medical Uses and Scientific Justifications|page=1047}}</ref>

===Genetics===
As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosome]]s, this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book | first= Claire | last=Austin | title= Irises: A Gardener's Encyclopedia | publisher= Timber Press, Incorporated | isbn = 978-0881927306 | year = 2005 | ol = OL8176432M | page=<!-- 274–275  in diff edition-->}}</ref>
It has had its chromosome counted several times; 2n=44, Banerji & Chaudhuri, 1972; 2n=28, Mao 1986; 2n=44 Sopova 1982; 2n=44, Váchová & Feráková, 1986 and 2n=44, Lovka, 1995.<ref name="America"/>

==Taxonomy==
It is most commonly known as '''bearded iris''' and in the UK occasionally as '''common German flag'''.<ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=''Iris germanica'' bearded iris |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9256/Iris-germanica/Details |website=rhs.org.uk |access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref>

It was first published and described as ''Iris germanica'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book '[[Species Plantarum]]' on page 38 in 1753.<ref name="plantlist"/><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title=''Iris germanica'' L., Sp. Pl. 1: 38 (1753) | url=https://www.ipni.org/n/438637-1 | publisher=ipni.org (International Plant Names Index) | access-date=4 May 2020}}</ref> It has since been shown to be a natural [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] involving a cross between two other European species (''[[Iris pallida]]'' and ''[[Iris variegata]]'') rather than a true wild species of Iris, with both parent species having the same chromosome number (2n = 24) as the hybrid offspring.<ref name="efloras">{{cite web |title=FNA Vol. 26 Page 373, 375, 376 |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200028171 |access-date=4 May 2020 |website=efloras.org (Flora of North America)}}</ref><ref name="pacbulb">{{cite web |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/index.php/GardenBeardedIrises |publisher=Pacific Bulb Society |title= Garden Bearded Irises |access-date=25 November 2014}}</ref>

As a hybrid, according to correct scientific nomenclature, its official [[Binomial nomenclature|Latin name]] is ''Iris x germanica,'' according to [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew]] and many other botanical authorities where cross 'x' denotes its hybrid status.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Iris × germanica'' L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:438637-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=29 July 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Iris'' × ''germanica'' – Species Details |url=https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=1850 |website=Atlas of Florida Plants |access-date=29 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Iris x germanica (IRIGE)[Overview]{{!}} EPPO Global Database |url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/IRIGE |access-date=2024-09-23 |website=gd.eppo.int}}</ref><ref name="grin" /> Despite this, ''Iris x germanica'' and its many named cultivars have been sold to gardeners under the name '''''Iris germanica''''' for many years, with some horticultural references, such as the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] (RHS) continuing to use ''Iris germanica'' as the accepted name.<ref name="gardenia" /><ref name="RHS" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Iris'' × ''germanica'' is thought to have originated in the Mediterranean region.<ref name=grin/><ref name="RHS"/> It is widely [[naturalized]] across Europe.<ref name="America"/>

==Cultivation==
It prefers to grow in full sun, with well-drained soil. It normally retains some of its leaves over the winter period. After it has flowered and during dry conditions through the summer is best time to divide and transplant.<ref name="America">{{cite web |last1=Laurin |first1=T. |title=(SPEC) ''Iris germanica'' L. |url=https://wiki.irises.org/Spec/SpecGermanica |access-date=4 May 2020 |date=6 May 2019}}</ref>

===Propagation===
It can be propagated by seed and by division.<ref name=efloras/>

===Hybrids and cultivars===

''I.'' × ''germanica'' var. ''amas'' was one of the most important cultivars in the creation of the modern tetraploid tall-bearded Irises.<ref name="America"/>

In Italy and Thailand, the leaves can be affected by a fungus, ''[[Torula masonii]]''.<ref name="Li2017">{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jun-Fu |last2=Phookamsak |first2=Rungtiwa |last3=Jeewon |first3=Rajesh |last4=Bhat |first4=Darbhe J. |last5=Mapook |first5=Ausana |last6=Camporesi |first6=Erio |last7=Shang |first7=Qiu-Ju |last8=Chukeatirote |first8=Ekachai |last9=Bahkali |first9=Ali H. |last10=Hyde |first10=Kevin D. |title=Molecular taxonomy and morphological characterization reveal new species and new host records of ''Torula'' species (Torulaceae, Pleosporales) |journal=Mycological Progress |date=2017 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=447–461|doi=10.1007/s11557-017-1292-2 }}</ref>

==In culture==
[[File:VanGogh-Irises 3.jpg|thumb|Irises by [[Vincent van Gogh]], 1890 ]]
In Iran and Kashmir,<ref name=irisbotanique>{{cite web |title=Chapter I Rhizomatous Iris (part 2) |url=http://irisbotanique.over-blog.com/article-chapitre-i-les-iris-rhizomateux-partie-2-123788250.html |publisher=irisbotanique.over-blog.com |access-date=20 October 2015}}</ref> ''[[Iris kashmiriana]]'' and ''Iris'' × ''germanica''<ref name=flowers>{{cite web |first=Gurcharan |last=Singh |title= Kashmir Iris |url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Kashmir%20Iris.html |publisher=flowersofindia.net |access-date=22 October 2015}}</ref> are commonly grown in [[Muslim]] places of burial such as [[Cemetery|cemeteries]].<ref name="ClaireAustin" /><ref name="british">British Iris Society (1997) {{Google books|pL6uPLo7l2gC|A Guide to Species Irises: Their Identification and Cultivation|page=38-39}}</ref><ref name="Trak">{{cite journal |last1=Trak |first1=Touseef Hussain |last2=Upadhayay |first2=Ravi |date=April 2015 |title=Ethnobotanical And Taxonomic Study of Members of Iridaceae Family of Kishtwar, (Jammu And Kashmir) India |url=http://www.ijpbs.net/cms/php/upload/4265_pdf.pdf |journal=International Journal of Pharma and Bio Sciences |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=779–793 |access-date=22 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160802023343/http://ijpbs.net/cms/php/upload/4265_pdf.pdf |archive-date=2 August 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=stebbings>{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |year=1997|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb|url-access=registration |location=Newton Abbot |publisher=David and Charles |page=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/23 23] |isbn=0715305395 }}</ref>

It has frequently been painted including 'Irises' (see right) and '[[Irises (painting)|Irises]]' both by [[Vincent van Gogh]] in 1890.<ref>Jennifer Helvey {{google books|LUZ-dHerY3sC|Irises: Vincent van Gogh in the Garden|page=21}}</ref>
